setup.zh: 舅舅送你走了三天；前一夜，你把最后半张饼分给了牛棚里的孙二狗。天没亮，河滩上一个穿白的人拿一块石头，买走了一个五六岁的孩子。三百级石阶直通云雾，顶上站着一个扫地的老头：「不看出身，不看荐书——只看三样：腿，脑子，胆子。」一试，腿：三百级，一炷香。
setup.en: Your uncle walked you three days; the night before, you gave the last half flatbread to Sun Ergou in the cowshed. Before dawn, on the riverbank, a man in white bought a child of five or six with a stone and an ingot. Three hundred stone steps climb into the clouds, and at the top stands an old sweeper: "Not by birth, not by letters of recommendation — by three things only: legs, head, nerve." First trial, legs: three hundred steps, one stick of incense.

recap.zh: 一试，三百级石阶：你三步一吸，三步一呼，替舅舅走了上来。
recap.en: First trial, three hundred steps: three steps a breath in, three a breath out, you climbed the stair for your uncle.

zh: 石阶顶上，一个扫地的老头。
en: Three hundred steps, straight into the clouds.
At the top, an old man with a broom.
First trial, legs: one stick of incense.

story.zh:
九月初七晌午，沈小满跟着舅舅，走在往泗水去的大路上，身后一阵吆喝，一顶滑竿从人堆当中颠了过去。四个轿夫抬着，前头两个家丁开道，把路上的人往两边赶；滑竿上坐着马小宝，手里一块桂花糕。滑竿边上走着马三，宽得像一扇门，一眼瞧见了路边的沈小满，站住了，笑道：「哟，沈家的也去？惦记沉鼎观那一年五两银子？」小满道：「惦记着呢，三爷。」马三的笑收了一收：谁都知道，家里有孩子进了仙门的，马家不敢收租。他拍了拍胸口，那里鼓鼓的，揣着一封信：「惦记也没用。我家小宝有这个。你进不去，今年的山风钱，翻一倍。」说罢，大步追滑竿去了。舅舅从头到尾没抬头，等他们走远了，才低声道：「还有两天。」

小满没接话。马家那封荐书，他倒不怎么怕；他心里最怕的，是一块石头。舅舅说，三试都过了，还要进正殿，把手按在一块测灵石上，那石头照着人身上的灵气亮，亮什么颜色，便是什么灵根。胸口木牌里的银月，临睡前只留给他一个字：「藏。」那石头要是一亮，亮出一道银光、亮出一条狐狸尾巴来，满殿的人都瞧见了——他不敢往下想。他问过木牌三回，木牌凉凉的，一回也没答。

越往南，路上往泗水去的人越多，到后来一眼望不到头，几千户人家，赶的是同一个日子。

九月初八傍晚，到了泗水边上。沉鼎山并不怎么高，只是陡，山腰以上笼着一层白雾，一道石阶从山脚笔直地插进雾里去，瞧不见尽头。石阶顶上，就是沉鼎观的山门。舅舅在河边站住了，望着那道石阶，望了很久，一个字也没讲。

山脚下的客栈早住满了，最好的一间上房，叫蒙山马家包了去。庙里的廊檐底下也躺满了人。廊柱边上生着一堆火，火边坐着一个汉子，三十出头，生得老相，一脸横肉，腰里别一把短刀，刀鞘上缠着红绸，是县城镖局的记号。他姓葛，行六，是马家雇来护送少爷的镖师。马家包了上房，没给他留铺，他便在廊下喝酒，喝的倒是马家的酒。

几个孩子围着火烤手，有个胆大的问他：「大叔，你也是来考的？」葛六笑了一声：「考过了。二十年前。」孩子们呼啦一下全围了上来。「考上了没有？」「考上了。外门，练气三层。」他从怀里摸出一颗核桃，两根指头一捏，「咔」的一声，碎了。满廊的人倒吸一口凉气。葛六把核桃仁丢进嘴里，道：「三层，就这点本事。练气九层，九层上头还有一道门槛，叫筑基，过了才算真踏进了仙门。我卡在三层六年，没上去，下山走镖。」

一个当爹的问：「那筑基……难么？」葛六伸出一根指头，在火边一圈孩子的脸上点过去：「你们这几千个，明天爬上去、测完了、进了门的，一百来个。一百来个里头，将来能筑基的——一个。」

廊下静了，火里一根柴「噼」地爆了一下。小满把「筑基」两个字在心里过了一遍。这两个字，他在那卷竹简的末一片上见过，娘念到那儿，说是盖房子；头一回有人说出它值多少。他憋不住，问道：「大叔，百日筑基——是不是一百天？」葛六看了他一眼，笑了：「百日，是打底子。底子跟地里的庄稼一样，白天你锄它、浇它，它是夜里自己长的；天天拔起苗来看，它就不长。我打了六年。」小满在心里把那富余的八十三天，一笔划掉了。

一个光脚的孩子忽然站起来，大声道：「那我就当那一个！」满廊的人都笑了。那孩子不笑，道：「我家七口人，二亩坡地，地一年比一年薄，今年种下去的豆子，收上来的比种下去的还少。我进了仙门，一年五两，够他们吃三年。」廊下又静了。葛六没笑，道：「……我当年，也这么说。」

他把酒葫芦往地上一顿，一抬眼，看见了坐在廊柱阴影里的舅舅，看了好一会儿，道：「这位老哥，面熟。二十年前，一百六十级，坐在那儿揉腿的，是你吧？我从你边上走上去的。」舅舅没说话。过了半晌，才道：「……是我。」葛六把酒葫芦朝他举了一举：「我走上去了，也就走到三层。」廊柱另一头的暗处，一个红鼻头的小姑娘拿炭条在一个蓝布面的本子上记了一笔：**一个。**谁也没注意她。

这时候一个马家的家丁挑着灯笼找了过来，道：「葛镖头，三爷叫你。」又压低了嗓子，「三爷问，你说的那个摆法，画好了没有？」葛六拍了拍胸口：「画好了。五两银子，一个格子也不差。」他站起身，跟着灯笼走了。小满不知道「摆法」是什么，只记住了「五两银子」和「格子」。马家的银子，花到哪里，从来不白花。

舅舅花了十个铜钱，在一户人家的牛棚里赁到半张草铺。牛棚里除了他们，还有一头牛，一对兖州来的父子，和一个一声不吭的瘦孩子。兖州那个爹是个嗓门大的，一进牛棚便拍着他儿子的肩膀跟人说，这孩子在村里赛跑，从没输过，明天那三百级，头一个冲上去的准是他。那瘦孩子十四五岁年纪，瘦得像一根晾衣竿，背着一个比他身子还大的包袱，腰里系着一个护身符，针脚密得看不见线，睡着了手还攥着。小满问他叫什么，他只说了两个字：「孙家。」再问，便不说了。

那天夜里，小满摸出了最后那张饼。明天要爬三百级、过三试，这是他最后一口干粮，吃完了，到明天晚上都未必有下一口。他掰下一半塞进嘴里，一抬头，草铺那头那个孙家的还醒着，正盯着他手里剩的那半张，喉头一动一动的。

小满看了看那半张饼，又看了看那孩子。他想起谷底那一夜，想起那只断了尾巴的小狐狸，想起他掰给它的那一半饼。他那时候想的是：它饿。他把手里那半张递了过去，道：「吃吧。明天要爬三百级呢。」那孩子愣了一愣，接过去，一口塞进嘴里，嚼得很快，嚼完了，才想起来说：「……谢谢。我叫孙二狗。」小满道：「沈小满。」孙二狗道：「我记着了。」

小满肚子里只剩半张饼，心里只有一块石头。

九月初九，是重阳。天还没亮透，泗水边的河滩上已经站满了人，雾贴着水面走，人的脸一张一张都是灰的。

河滩当中让出了一块空地。空地上站着一个人，一身白袍，白得在这一河滩的泥里不沾一点泥。他手里托着一块灰石头，鸡蛋大小，跟前排着一溜小孩子，大的七八岁，小的还要人抱着，都是爹娘一早领来的。他把那块石头往孩子的手心里一按，按一下，看一眼，摇摇头，下一个。他从头到尾，一声不出。

排到一个石匠模样的汉子，领着两个儿子。大的那个十二三岁，又黑又壮，一双手跟他爹一样，指节上全是老茧，石头按上去，灰扑扑的，什么也没亮。白衣人摇了摇头。小的那个五六岁，还拖着鼻涕，石头一按上去，忽地亮了——亮成一片青，青得像开春头一茬麦苗，一种颜色，干干净净，一点杂色也没有。河滩上「嗡」的一声。

白衣人这才点了点头，从袖子里摸出一锭银子，放进那汉子的手心里，开口说了两个字：「收着。」小满离得近，看见了那锭银子翻过来的底：錾着一个记号，一个圈，圈里一横。

他身上一凉。那记号他见过。谷底那个摔断了腰的锁儿，领口里缝着的，就是这样一锭——那一锭，这时候正揣在他怀里。他隔着衣裳摸了一摸，硬的，凉的。

这一身白，这两个字的嗓子，又干又深，像有人趴在老井口上往底下喊——小满认得：去年冬月廿二进村问他「围脖呢？」的，就是这个人。小满往人堆后头缩了半步，缩到一个挑担子的汉子身后。胸口的木牌冰凉，一动不动。他想起爹在柴垛顶上说的那一句：它听见的不是你喘，是你心慌。他便把一口气吐得又细又长，吐到底，再慢慢吸回来。那白衣人从头到尾，没往这边看一眼。

那汉子捧着银子，跪下去，给白衣人磕了一个头；又转过身，给他那个小儿子磕了一个头。小孩子不懂，看着他爹的后脑勺，咯咯地笑。白衣人把他抱起来，往河岸上走，岸上停着一辆青篷马车。走到半路，那孩子才觉出不对来，在白衣人怀里扭着身子，伸着两只手，哇地哭了：「哥——」

那个大的追了两步，给他爹一把揪住了领子。马车走了。岸边站着一个五十上下的人，灰袍，生着一张没睡醒的脸，白衣人上车之前，冲他点了一点头，他也点了一点头，打了个呵欠，转身往石阶那边去了。

人堆里有人小声道：「太华山上的太一宫来的。天下头一号的仙门，隔几年来一回，专挑一种颜色的娃娃。」又有人道：「一锭，十两。」

石匠把那锭银子揣进怀里，揣得很深，回头对大儿子道：「你也上去。考上了，一年五两；考不上，别回来。家里还有三张嘴。」说完，他往北走了，一次也没有回头。

那大孩子站在河滩上，没有哭。他转过脸来，看见小满正看着他，便道：「那石头……亮了，就是仙人要的？」小满道：「……嗯。」那孩子道：「他们把小豆带哪儿去了？」小满答不上来。那孩子低头看了看自己的手，那一双手刚才按在石头上，石头没亮。他道：「我要是也亮了，他们就把我也带去了。」

小满问他叫什么。他道：「石蛋。」

辰时还没到，石阶底下已经挤得水泄不通。卖炊饼的、卖茶水的，还有卖「登仙符」的——一张黄纸，画几道红杠，说是贴在腿肚子上，登石阶不喘气，十文钱一张——在人缝里钻来钻去，生意好得出奇。舅舅在那卖符的跟前站了半天，终于没有买，回头对小满道：「这个，是骗人的。」小满道：「您怎么知道？」舅舅道：「我当年贴了三张。」

石阶底下，拿绳子圈了一片空地，十几个穿灰袍的执事站在里头，查验年纪（十二起）、籍贯，一人发一块竹牌，叫作考牌，拿烧红的铁签子当场烙上名字。唱名的那个执事，五十上下，生着一张没睡醒的脸，一面唱名，一面打呵欠——小满认得这张脸：天不亮的时候，河滩上，白衣人上马车之前冲他点过一点头的，就是他。他拿竹牌敲着手心道：「三试，一试画一道。三道画满，进正殿测灵；牌子丢了，便算你没来过。有荐书的，哪一试没过，许补——怎么补，执事说了算。」刀剑弓棍一律解下来，挂在一面木架上，拿竹签子记了名字，说是傍晚抬上山门，入了门的自己去领。小满把爷爷那张弓挂了上去，缠满牛筋的弓背夹在一排亮闪闪的刀剑中间，活像一条打了补丁的裤子混在一群新衣裳里。小满记住了那弓挂在第三排左数第七个，把考牌揣进怀里，贴着那块木牌。

便在这时，人群后头一阵骚动：「让一让！马家少爷来了！」马家的滑竿到了，一个家丁给马小宝打伞，一个给他扇扇子——这一天既没下雨，也没出太阳。马三跟在滑竿边上，时不时隔着衣裳按一按怀里那封信，像按着一只会飞的鸟。滑竿后头，走着葛六。马小宝一眼瞧见了小满，冲他扬了扬下巴：「哟，沈小满，你们家那扇门，扛回来没有？」小满道：「扛回来了，小宝哥。装得有点歪。」

辰时正，山门上「当」的一声钟，几千个孩子霎时间静了下来。石阶顶上，不知什么时候站了一个扫地的老头，一身灰布短褂，拄着一把竹扫帚，佝偻着背，看都不看底下一眼，只顾一下一下地扫他脚底下那一级台阶。那是第三百级。观里的老弟子说，这老头扫这一级扫了五十年，旁的台阶落了叶子、积了雪，他一概不管。扫了好一会儿，他才开口，声音不高，一个字一个字清清楚楚地落到山脚下来：「沉鼎观收人。不看出身，不看荐书——」人群里「嗡」的一声。马三的那只手，僵在了胸口上。那老头接着道：「——只看三样。腿。脑子。胆子。」说完，他又低头扫地。

舅舅在人群里挤到小满跟前，一把抓住他的胳膊，压低了嗓子道：「记着，别冲！还有——上去以后，别往底下看。」小满道：「为什么？」舅舅张了张嘴，道：「……底下有我。」

石阶顶上，一个执事点着了一炷香，插在一只铜炉里，喊了一声：「开始！」

一试考腿：三百级石阶，一级齐膝高，一炷香。「开始」两个字还没落地，几千个孩子便一窝蜂地往上冲，你推我搡，喊爹的、喊娘的、踩了别人鞋的、给别人踩了鞋的，乱成一锅粥，活像一群给人打开了笼门的鸭子。绳子外头，爹娘们喊名字的声音一浪高过一浪：「二牛——慢点——」「宝儿，别回头——」「三步一口气——」这最后一句，是舅舅喊的。他喊得脖子上的青筋都鼓了起来，喊完了，自己先愣了一愣，像是没想到这几个字，隔了二十年，会从自己嘴里喊出来。
story.en:
Noon on the seventh of the ninth month: Shen Xiaoman and his uncle were on the high road to the Si. A shout from behind, and a sedan chair came jolting straight through the crowd — four bearers, two servants in front clearing the way, pushing people to either side; in the chair sat Ma Xiaobao, an osmanthus cake in hand. Beside it walked Ma San, broad as a door. He spotted Xiaoman at the roadside, stopped, and grinned. "Well, the Shens are going too? Got your eye on Chending Temple's five taels a year?" Xiaoman said, "I have, Third Master." Ma San's grin shrank a little: everyone knew the Mas daren't take rent from a family with a child inside the immortal gate. He patted his chest, which bulged with a letter. "Eyes won't help. My Xiaobao has this. You don't get in, this year's mountain-wind money doubles." And off he strode after the chair. His uncle never once looked up; only when they were well gone did he say, low: "Two days left."

Xiaoman didn't answer. The Ma family's letter didn't frighten him much. What he feared most was a stone. His uncle said that once the three trials were passed you went into the main hall and put your hand on a spirit-testing stone, and the stone lit by the spirit in you: whatever colours it showed, that was your root. Yinyue, asleep in the token on his chest, had left him one word before she slept: "Hide." If that stone lit up and showed a streak of silver, a fox's tail, with the whole hall watching — he didn't dare think further. He had asked the token three times. It stayed cool, and never answered once.

The farther south, the more people on the road bound for the Si, until there was no end to them — several thousand households, racing the same day.

At dusk on the eighth they reached the Si. Mount Chending wasn't very high, only steep, wrapped in white mist from the waist up, and a stone stair ran straight from its foot into the mist, no end in sight. At the top of the stair stood the gate of Chending Temple. His uncle stopped on the bank and looked at the stair a long time, without a word.

The inns at the foot of the mountain were long since full — the best upstairs room taken by the Ma family of Mount Meng — and the temple veranda was full of people lying down too. By a pillar burned a fire, and beside it sat a man just past thirty who looked older, heavy-jowled, a short knife at his belt, its sheath wound in red silk: the mark of the county escort bureau. His name was Ge, sixth son — the escort the Mas had hired to see the young master there. The Mas had taken the good room and left him no bed, so he drank under the veranda. The wine, at least, was the Mas'.

A few children were warming their hands at the fire, and a bold one asked him: "Uncle, did you come to sit the trials too?" Ge Liu laughed. "Sat them already. Twenty years ago." The children crowded round in a rush. "Did you get in?" "Got in. Outer court, third level of qi refining." He took a walnut from his coat and pinched it between two fingers — *crack* — and it broke. The whole veranda drew in its breath. Ge Liu tossed the kernel into his mouth. "Third level, and that's all it's good for. Qi refining has nine levels, and above the ninth there's one more threshold, called foundation building; cross it and you're truly through the immortal gate. I was stuck at the third for six years, never got past, and came down the mountain to guard caravans."

A father asked, "And this foundation building… is it hard?" Ge Liu held up one finger and pointed it round the ring of children's faces by the fire. "You few thousand — the ones who climb up tomorrow, get tested and get through the gate: a hundred or so. Out of that hundred or so, the ones who'll ever build a foundation — one."

The veranda went quiet; a stick in the fire popped. Xiaoman turned the words "foundation building" over in his mind. He had seen them on the last slip of that bamboo scroll; when his mother read that far she said it meant building a house. This was the first time anyone had said what it was worth. He couldn't hold it in. "Uncle — a hundred days to build a foundation — is that really a hundred days?" Ge Liu looked at him and laughed. "A hundred days is laying the groundwork. Groundwork is like a crop in the field: by day you hoe it and water it, and it grows by itself at night. Pull the seedling up every day to look, and it won't grow. I laid mine for six years." In his head Xiaoman crossed out the eighty-three spare days with one stroke.

A barefoot boy suddenly stood up and said loudly, "Then I'll be that one!" The whole veranda laughed. The boy didn't. "Seven mouths at home, two mu of hillside, and the land thinner every year. This year the beans we harvested came to less than the beans we sowed. If I get through the gate, five taels a year — that feeds them three years." The veranda went quiet again. Ge Liu didn't laugh. "…I said that too, once."

He set his wine gourd down hard, glanced up, and saw the uncle sitting in the shadow of a pillar. He looked a good while. "You, old brother — I know your face. Twenty years ago, the hundred-and-sixtieth step, sitting there rubbing your legs — that was you, wasn't it? I walked past you on the way up." The uncle said nothing. After a long while he said, "…It was me." Ge Liu raised the gourd to him. "I walked on up, and only got as far as the third level." In the dark at the other end of the veranda a little girl with a red nose made a note in a blue cloth-covered notebook with a stick of charcoal: **One.** Nobody noticed her.

Just then a Ma servant came looking with a lantern. "Escort Ge, Third Master wants you." And lower: "Third Master asks — that layout you told him of, have you drawn it?" Ge Liu patted his chest. "Drawn. Five taels, not one square off." He got up and followed the lantern. Xiaoman didn't know what a "layout" was; he only remembered "five taels" and "squares". Ma money, wherever it went, was never spent for nothing.

For ten coppers his uncle rented half a straw bed in someone's cowshed. Besides them the shed held a cow, a father and son from Yanzhou, and a thin boy who never said a word. The Yanzhou father was a loud one; the moment he came in he slapped his son's shoulder and told everyone the boy had never lost a race in the village, and the first one up those three hundred steps tomorrow would be him. The thin boy was fourteen or fifteen, thin as a laundry pole, carrying a bundle bigger than himself, a charm tied at his waist with stitches so fine you couldn't see the thread; asleep, he still gripped it. Xiaoman asked his name; he said only two words: "Sun family." Asked again, he said nothing.

That night Xiaoman took out the last flatbread. Tomorrow meant three hundred steps and three trials; this was his last food, and once it was gone there might be nothing till tomorrow night. He broke off half and put it in his mouth, and looked up: at the far end of the straw the Sun boy was still awake, staring at the half left in his hand, his throat working.

Xiaoman looked at the half flatbread, and at the boy. He remembered that night at the bottom of the valley, the little fox with its broken tails, the half flatbread he had broken off for it. What he'd thought then was: it's hungry. He held out the half. "Eat. We've three hundred steps to climb tomorrow." The boy stared a moment, took it, stuffed it in whole and chewed fast, and only when he'd swallowed remembered to say: "…Thank you. I'm Sun Ergou." Xiaoman said, "Shen Xiaoman." Sun Ergou said, "I'll remember."

Xiaoman had only half a flatbread in his belly, and a stone on his mind.

The ninth of the ninth month was the Double Ninth. It wasn't yet properly light, and the flats by the Si were already packed with people; the mist walked along the water, and every face was grey.

In the middle of the flats a space had been cleared. In it stood a man in a white robe, so white that in all that riverbank mud not a speck clung to it. On his palm he held a grey stone the size of a hen's egg, and before him stood a line of small children, the eldest seven or eight, the youngest still carried, each brought down early by a father or mother. He pressed the stone into each child's palm — a press, a look, a shake of the head, next. From first to last he made no sound.

Then came a man who looked like a stonemason, with two sons. The elder was twelve or thirteen, dark and sturdy, his hands like his father's, calloused at every knuckle; the stone pressed into them stayed dusty grey and lit nothing. The man in white shook his head. The younger was five or six, his nose still running; the moment the stone touched him it lit — lit a sheet of green, green as the first wheat shoots of spring, a single colour, clean, without a fleck of anything else. A murmur went over the flats.

Only then did the man in white nod. He took a silver ingot from his sleeve, set it in the mason's palm, and only then spoke — two words: "Keep it." Xiaoman was close enough to see the underside as it turned: a mark struck into it — a circle, with a bar across the middle.

He went cold. He had seen that mark. Down in the valley, the boy Suo'er with his back broken had had one just like it sewn inside his collar — and that very ingot was in Xiaoman's coat right now. He touched it through the cloth: hard, cold.

That white, and the voice behind those two words — dry and deep, like someone calling down into an old well — Xiaoman knew them: the one who came into the village on the twenty-second of the eleventh month and asked him "Where's the scarf?" was this very man. Xiaoman shrank half a step back into the crowd, behind a man with a carrying pole. The token on his chest was icy and did not stir. He remembered what his father had said on top of the woodpile: it doesn't hear you panting, it hears your heart racing. So he let a breath out thin and long, all the way, and slowly drew it back in. From first to last the man in white never looked his way.

The mason, holding the silver, knelt and knocked his head once to the man in white; then he turned and knocked his head once to his little son. The little boy didn't understand; he looked at the back of his father's head and giggled. The man in white picked him up and walked toward the bank, where a covered cart with a blue awning stood waiting. Halfway there the child sensed something wrong, twisted in the man's arms, reached out both hands, and burst into tears: "Brother —"

The elder boy ran two steps and was caught by the collar by his father. The cart left. On the bank stood a man of fifty or so in a grey robe, with a face that looked as if it had never quite woken up; before the man in white climbed in, he gave the grey robe a nod, and the grey robe nodded back, yawned, and turned away toward the stair.

Someone in the crowd said under his breath: "From the Taiyi Palace, up on Mount Taihua. The first sect under heaven — comes every few years, and picks out only the one-colour babies." Someone else said, "One ingot — ten taels."

The mason tucked the ingot into his coat, deep, and turned to his elder son. "You go up too. Get in, it's five taels a year; don't get in, don't come back. There are three more mouths at home." With that he walked off north, and not once did he look back.

The elder boy stood on the flats and didn't cry. He turned his face, saw Xiaoman looking at him, and said, "That stone… if it lights, that's what the immortals want?" Xiaoman said, "…Yes." The boy said, "Where are they taking Little Dou?" Xiaoman couldn't answer. The boy looked down at his own hands — they had been pressed to the stone just now, and it hadn't lit. He said, "If mine had lit, they'd have taken me too."

Xiaoman asked his name. He said, "Shidan."

Before the hour of Chen, the foot of the stair was packed so tight not a drop of water could get through. Sellers of griddle cakes, sellers of tea, and sellers of "Ascension Charms" — a sheet of yellow paper with a few red strokes on it; stick it on your calf and you'll climb the stair without panting, ten coppers a sheet — wormed through the cracks in the crowd, doing a roaring trade. His uncle stood in front of the charm seller a long while, in the end didn't buy, and turned to Xiaoman: "These are a swindle." Xiaoman said, "How do you know?" His uncle said, "I stuck on three, that year."

At the foot of the stair a space was roped off, and a dozen stewards in grey robes stood inside checking age (twelve and up) and home county, handing each child a bamboo slip called a trial tag and burning the name into it on the spot with a red-hot iron spike. The steward calling the names, fifty or so, with a face that looked as if it had never quite woken up, yawned between names — Xiaoman knew that face: before dawn, on the flats, the man in white had nodded to him before climbing into the cart. He tapped a slip on his palm. "Three trials, one stroke for each. Three strokes full, and you go into the main hall to be tested; lose your tag, and you were never here. Those with a letter of recommendation who fail a trial may make it up — how to make it up, the steward decides." Swords, knives, bows and staves all had to come off and hang on a wooden rack, tagged with a bamboo name slip; they'd be carried up to the gate at dusk, and those who got in could fetch their own. Xiaoman hung his grandfather's bow on it — the ox-sinew-wrapped back squeezed between a row of shining blades like a pair of patched trousers among new clothes. Xiaoman marked that it hung third row, seventh from the left, tucked his tag inside his coat against the wooden token.

Just then there was a stir at the back of the crowd: "Make way! Make way! The young Ma master's here!" The Ma sedan chair had arrived, one servant holding a parasol over Ma Xiaobao, another fanning him — on a day with neither rain nor sun. Ma San walked beside the chair, now and then pressing the letter in his coat through the cloth, as if pressing down a bird that might fly. Behind the chair walked Ge Liu. Ma Xiaobao spotted Xiaoman and jerked his chin. "Well, Shen Xiaoman — that door of yours, did you carry it home?" Xiaoman said, "We did, Xiaobao-ge. Put it back a bit crooked."

At the hour of the dragon a bell struck over the gate — *dang* — and several thousand children fell silent at once. At the top of the stair, no one knew since when, stood an old man with a broom: a grey cloth jacket, a bamboo broom to lean on, a bent back; he didn't look down once, only swept the step under his feet, stroke after stroke. That was the three hundredth. The temple's old disciples said he had swept that one step for fifty years; leaves and snow on the others he left alone. After a good while he spoke, not loudly, each word falling clear to the foot of the mountain: "Chending Temple takes disciples. Not by birth, not by letters of recommendation —" The crowd hummed. Ma San's hand froze on his chest. The old man went on: "— by three things only. Legs. Head. Nerve." That said, he bent to his sweeping again.

His uncle pushed through the crowd to Xiaoman, gripped his arm, and said under his breath: "Remember — don't charge! And — once you're up, don't look down." Xiaoman said, "Why?" His uncle opened his mouth. "…I'll be down there."

At the top of the stair a steward lit a stick of incense, set it in a bronze burner, and called out: "Begin!"

The first trial tested legs: three hundred stone steps, each knee-high, one stick of incense. Before "Begin" had even landed, several thousand children surged up in a mob, pushing and shoving, shouting for dads and mums, treading on shoes and trodden on, a pot of porridge, like ducks when someone opens the cage. Outside the rope, the parents' shouting rose wave on wave: "Erniu — slow down —" "Bao'er, don't look back —" "Three steps a breath —" That last was his uncle. He shouted till the veins stood out on his neck, and then stopped short himself, as if he hadn't expected those words, twenty years on, to come out of his own mouth.

label.en: At the back: three steps in, three steps out

story.zh:
沈小满却没有冲。他走在最后面。他爹教过他：追兔子比快，追鹿比稳；上山的路，是山的，你跟山抢，山不让你。他冲由他冲，石阶三百级；他快由他快，香只一炷香——小满心里把这两句颠来倒去地念，一级一级地走，三步一吸，三步一呼，只看脚底下这一级。

冲在最前头的那些孩子，到了一百级上下，一个一个便像腿上绑了石头：有的坐在台阶上喘，喘得张着嘴直不起腰；有的扶着崖壁，一步一挪。马小宝是两个家丁一左一右架上来的，那扫地老头在石阶顶上远远看了一眼，家丁便松了手，他在一百二十级坐下了——他家有荐书。小满从他身边走过去，没有停。

走到一百三十级上下，他看见了牛棚里那个兖州来的孩子。那孩子是跟着头一拨冲上去的，这时候扶着崖壁，脸白得像一张纸，两条腿抖得像筛糠。他看见小满，眼睛一亮，像是看见了一根救命的绳子，喊道：「兄弟！拉我一把！」

小满是想拉的。可他知道，这一拉，他三步一吸、三步一呼的那口气就断了；气一断，他自己也要在这里坐下。他爹说过，山里遇见别人掉进坑里，先看看自己脚底下站稳了没有；自己都没站稳，伸手去拉，是两个人一起掉进去。小满便没有伸手，只道：「别冲了。三步一口气。跟着我的脚。」那孩子跟着他走了十来级，到了一百四十级，终于还是一屁股坐了下去，摆着手道：「兄弟，你走，你走……」小满回头看了他一眼，走了。走出去十几级，他听见身后那孩子在哭，哭得很小声，像是怕人听见。他没有回头，心里却想：等我哪一天站得够稳了，我要拉。拉得动几个，拉几个。这念头一闪就过去了，他那时候并没有当真。

走到一百五十级，一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘从他身边冲了过去。她没坐下，也没哭，他只看见一个鼻头冻得通红的侧脸，咬着牙，一口气往上冲，冲得小辫子一甩一甩的。小满心里一跳：阿禾？临走前些日子，她在井台边上拦住他，问泗水几天的路、一天吃几张饼，记在一个他从没见过的本子上——他还当她是替她爹问的。他喊了一声：「阿禾！」那姑娘没回头，一口气冲进雾里去了。往上又走了几级，一个黑壮的身影也从他边上闷着头擦过去，指节上全是老茧，是石蛋。他不喘，也不看人，一步一步踩得极重，像是要把石阶踩进山里去。

一百六十级到了。这一级台阶，同别的台阶没什么两样，只是边上的崖壁上，不知什么年月，给人用石头、用刀、用指甲，刻满了密密麻麻的字，一层压着一层，有的是名字，有的是年月，有的只是一道杠——都是在这一级上坐下过的人刻的。小满跨过去的时候，扭过头朝那些刻痕里多看了一眼。他不知道自己在找什么。他没有找到。

过了一百六十级，石阶便陡了，一级比一级高出半指，攒到两百级上下，攒成了一道梯子；两边的崖壁也挨近了，窄处只容两个人侧着身子过。他不往上看，也不往下看，只数：一吸，二吸，三吸；抬脚，落脚，再抬脚。雾里远远传来一下一下的沙沙声，是扫帚扫在青石上的声音，他走一级，它便近一分。

走到两百六十级上下，身后忽然一阵吆喝：「让开！让开！」是那顶滑竿，又上来了。原来马三在石阶底下，把那封信亮了出来。执事看了一眼落款，道：「荐书。许补。」四个轿夫便抬着马小宝，一路颠上来。滑竿挤过小满身边，把他挤在崖壁上，蹭破了一块皮。挤过去了，却在前头最窄的那一段停住了。马小宝在滑竿上回过头来，冲他咧嘴一笑：「慢点抬。本少爷看看风景。」

雾里什么风景也没有。四个轿夫横在石阶上，前后堵得严严实实，一只猫也钻不过去。小满抬头看——看不见铜炉，雾太厚。可他算得出来：那炷香，这时候怕是只剩一截指头了。

他站在那里想了一想。他爹说过，堵在前头的东西，不一定要翻过去。他把身子一矮，趴在石阶上，从前头两个轿夫的腿缝里、从滑竿的杠子底下，像钻灌木丛撵獾子一样，一骨碌钻了过去。滑竿一晃。等马小宝回过头来找人，小满已经在五级之上了。马小宝却没有喊，他低头瞧着滑竿底下的石阶，瞧见了一样东西，伸手捞了起来，塞进了袖子里。小满回头瞧见了，没顾上多想。

最后那几十级，是在雾里走的。走着走着，雾一下子薄了。他抬起头来，只见雾在他脚底下，一整片的白，平平地铺开去，一直铺到天边，蒙山、泗水、县城、石坳村，统统给盖在了底下；雾上头，是明晃晃的太阳，是一层一层的殿宇，飞檐一角一角地翘起来，像一群正要起飞的鸟。他只看了一眼，便又低下头——最后一级到了。

那一级，就是扫地老头扫的那一级，青石面上亮得能照见天。先上来的那几百个孩子，一个一个踩上去，踩出一片泥脚印，那老头便跟在后头，一下一下地扫。小满低头看了看自己的草鞋：走了三天的路，沾满了泥，前头还破了一个洞，一个脚趾头从洞里探出来。石坪上，守着铜炉的执事已经举起了手。小满抬起脚，又放下了，弯下腰，把草鞋底在上一级台阶的边沿上刮了刮，刮一下，看一看，又刮一下，刮干净了，这才抬脚，轻轻地踩了上去。扫地的老头正扫到他身边，扫帚停了一停。

执事的手落了下来：「香尽！」炉里最后一截香灰，恰在他那只脚落地的时候，断了。

执事走过来，伸手道：「考牌。」小满往怀里一摸——木牌还在，考牌没了。他把衣裳里里外外摸了三遍，摸出一身冷汗。执事等了一等，道：「牌子丢了，便算你没来过。」说着便要往下一个人那里走。

便在这时，那顶滑竿也上来了。小满想起滑竿底下，马小宝弯腰捞进袖子里的那样东西，道：「执事，我的考牌，在马少爷袖子里。」马小宝在滑竿上嚷道：「胡说！」扫地的老头正扫到滑竿边上，扫帚「笃」的一声，不轻不重，敲在滑竿的杠子上。滑竿一颤，马小宝的袖子一抖，一块竹牌「啪」地落在青石上。执事捡起来，看了一眼上头烙的名字，递给小满，画了一道。扫地的老头一个字也没说，又低头扫地。

小满站在石坪边上，终于还是没忍住，回过头去往下看了一眼。石阶一路垂下去，隐进白雾里，雾的底下，是几千个爹和娘，小得像地上的芝麻，哪一粒是舅舅，他一点也瞧不出来。一转头，那扫地的老头拄着扫帚，第一次抬起眼皮，正看着他——看他的脚，又看他的胸口，看他一起一伏的那口气。

小满心里「咯噔」一下。三百级走下来，他的气还是匀的——他洗过髓，又练了一冬的吐纳，这老头看得出来么？他赶紧张大了嘴，呼哧呼哧地喘起粗气来，喘得跟方才那些坐在台阶上的孩子一模一样，一面喘，一面拿袖子擦汗，擦得十分卖力。扫地的老头看了他一会儿，道：「喘得好。」又扫地了。小满到底也没弄明白，这三个字，是夸他喘，还是夸他装。
story.en:
Shen Xiaoman didn't charge. He walked at the very back. His father had taught him: chasing rabbits you race for speed, chasing deer you race for steadiness; the road up a mountain belongs to the mountain, race the mountain and it won't let you by. Let them charge — the stair is three hundred steps; let them hurry — the incense is one stick: Xiaoman turned the two lines over and over in his head, walking step by step, three steps a breath in, three a breath out, looking only at the step under his feet.

The children charging out in front, round about the hundredth step, one after another seemed to have stones tied to their legs: some sat on the steps panting, mouths open, unable to straighten; some leaned on the cliff wall and shuffled step by step. Ma Xiaobao was carried up between two servants, one at each arm; the old sweeper glanced down from the top of the stair, the servants let go, and he sat down on the hundred-and-twentieth step — his family had a letter. Xiaoman walked past him and didn't stop.

Around step one hundred and thirty he saw the Yanzhou boy from the cowshed. The boy had charged up with the first wave, and now clung to the cliff wall, face white as paper, legs shaking like sieves. Seeing Xiaoman, his eyes lit as if at a rope thrown to a drowning man. "Brother! Pull me up!"

Xiaoman wanted to pull. But he knew that if he did, the breath of three steps in and three out would break; break the breath, and he'd be sitting down here himself. His father had said: when you meet someone fallen into a pit in the mountains, first see if your own feet are steady; if you're not steady yourself and reach out to pull, the two of you fall in together. So Xiaoman didn't reach out. He said only: "Stop charging. Three steps a breath. Follow my feet." The boy followed him a dozen steps, and at step one hundred and forty sat down after all, waving his hands. "Brother, you go, you go…" Xiaoman looked back at him once, and went. A dozen steps further up he heard the boy crying behind him, very quietly, as though afraid of being heard. He didn't look back; but he thought: the day I'm standing steady enough, I'll pull. As many as I can pull, I'll pull. The thought flashed and was gone; he didn't take it seriously then.

At the hundred-and-fiftieth step a girl with two little braids rushed past him. She didn't sit down and she didn't cry; all he saw was a profile with a nose frozen red, teeth gritted, charging up in one breath, braids flicking. Xiaoman's heart jumped: Ah He? A few days before he left she had stopped him at the well and asked how many days to the Si and how many flatbreads a day, and written it in a notebook he'd never seen — he'd thought she was asking for her father. He called, "Ah He!" The girl didn't look back; she charged straight up into the mist. A few steps higher, a dark, sturdy figure brushed past him too, head down, calloused at every knuckle — Shidan. He wasn't panting and he didn't look at anyone; every step came down hard, as if he meant to drive the stair into the mountain.

Step one hundred and sixty. It was no different from the other steps — only the cliff wall beside it had been carved, in who knew what years, with stones, with knives, with fingernails, crowded with writing, layer on layer: names, years, sometimes a single stroke — all carved by people who had sat down on this step. As he crossed it Xiaoman turned his head and looked once more among the carvings. He didn't know what he was looking for. He didn't find it.

Past one hundred and sixty the stair turned steep, each step half a finger higher than the one below, adding up by two hundred into a ladder; the cliff walls closed in, the narrow places only wide enough for two people sideways. He looked neither up nor down, only counted: one breath, two, three; lift the foot, set it down, lift again. From somewhere in the mist came a steady *shh, shh* — a broom on bluestone; with every step he climbed, it came a little nearer.

Around step two hundred and sixty there was a shout behind him: "Make way! Make way!" It was that sedan chair, coming up again. At the foot of the stair, it turned out, Ma San had brought out the letter; the steward glanced at the name it was signed with and said, "A letter. He may make it up." So the four bearers carried Ma Xiaobao up, jolting all the way, cake crumbs all over him. The chair squeezed past Xiaoman, pinning him to the cliff wall and scraping off a patch of skin. Having squeezed past, it stopped dead in the narrowest stretch ahead. Ma Xiaobao turned round in the chair and grinned at him. "Carry me slow. This young master's enjoying the view."

There was no view in the mist. The four bearers stood across the stair, front and back, blocking it so tight not a cat could get by. Xiaoman looked up — he couldn't see the burner; the mist was too thick. But he could reckon it: that stick of incense must be down to a finger's width by now.

He stood and thought a moment. His father had said: whatever blocks your way, you don't always have to go over it. He ducked low, dropped flat on the steps, and between the legs of the two front bearers, under the chair poles, the way you crawl through brush after a badger, rolled through. The chair lurched; Ma Xiaobao yelped, and his osmanthus cake dropped. By the time he turned round to look for him, Xiaoman was five steps above. Ma Xiaobao didn't shout, though. He was looking at the step under the chair; he'd seen something there. He reached down, scooped it up, and tucked it in his sleeve.

The last few dozen steps were climbed in mist. As he walked the mist suddenly thinned. He looked up: the mist lay under his feet, one sheet of white spread flat to the edge of the sky, Mount Meng, the Si, the county town, Shi'ao Village all covered beneath it; above it the blazing sun, and hall upon hall, the eaves tilting up corner after corner like a flock of birds about to take off. He looked just once, and lowered his head again — the last step had come.

That step was the one the old sweeper swept, the bluestone bright enough to reflect the sky. The several hundred children who'd come up first had trodden on it one by one and left a sheet of muddy footprints, and the old man followed after them, sweeping stroke by stroke. Xiaoman looked down at his straw sandals: three days of road, caked in mud, a hole in the front with one toe poking out. On the terrace, the steward watching the burner had raised his hand. Xiaoman lifted his foot, then set it down again; bent over, scraped the sandal soles on the edge of the step below, scraped once, looked, scraped again, and when they were clean, lifted his foot and set it lightly on the step. The old sweeper, sweeping beside him just then, paused his broom.

The steward's hand came down: "The incense is out!" The last stub of ash in the burner broke just as that foot touched stone.

The steward came over and held out his hand. "Tag." Xiaoman felt inside his jacket — the wooden token was there; the trial tag was gone. He searched his clothes inside and out three times and came up with nothing but a cold sweat. The steward waited a moment. "Lose the tag and you were never here." And he turned to go to the next child.

Just then the sedan chair came up too. As it passed the old sweeper, the broom came down — *tok* — neither hard nor soft, on the chair's pole. The chair shook, Ma Xiaobao's sleeve shook, and something fell with a *clack* on the bluestone: a bamboo tally. The old sweeper bent, picked it up, glanced at the name branded on it, and without a word put it into Xiaoman's hand. Ma Xiaobao shouted from the chair: "I found it! I picked it up on the steps!" The old sweeper looked at him once. "Made it up." And bent to his sweeping again. The steward took Xiaoman's tag and drew one stroke on it.

Xiaoman stood at the edge of the terrace, and in the end couldn't help looking back down once. The stair hung down and vanished into white mist, and under the mist were several thousand fathers and mothers, small as sesame seeds; which seed was his uncle he couldn't tell at all. He turned round, and the old sweeper, leaning on his broom, had raised his eyelids for the first time and was looking at him — at his feet, then at his chest, at the breath rising and falling there.

Xiaoman's heart gave a jolt. Three hundred steps, and his breath was still even — he'd had his marrow washed, and a winter of breathing practice; could this old man tell? He quickly opened his mouth wide and panted, huffing and puffing just like the children who'd been sitting on the steps, mopping sweat with his sleeve as he panted, very diligently. The old sweeper looked at him a while. "Well panted." And swept again. Xiaoman never did work out whether that meant the panting, or the pretending.

exits.means: rushes up the steps as fast as possible

story.zh:
小满也冲了。几千只鸭子里，多他一只不多。

冲到一百五十级上下，他的腿忽然沉了——不是累，是像有人往他两条腿上，一边挂了一块磨盘，越急，磨盘越重。身边的孩子一个接一个地坐下去，有的喘，有的哭。

走到一百五十级的时候，他从一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘身边走过去——不对，是那姑娘从他身边冲过去。她没坐下，也没哭，冲过他身边的时候，他只看见一个鼻头冻得通红的侧脸，像一根萝卜，咬着牙，一口气往上冲，冲得小辫子一甩一甩的。那个背影，瞧着有点眼熟。小满想多看两眼，她已经冲上去了，只剩一截小辫子在雾里一晃，就没了。

一百六十级。他停下来，扶着膝盖，大口大口地喘气。崖壁上刻满了字，都是在这一级上坐下过的人刻的。二十年前，舅舅在这儿坐了一炷香，看着别人一个一个从他身边走过去。

他想起他爹说的：追一头鹿，越急，鹿跑得越远。他站直了，三步一吸，三步一呼，不快，也不停。

香只剩一指的时候，他站在了第三百级石阶上，两条腿抖得像两根面条。扫地的老头抬起眼皮，看了他一眼，那一眼的意思大约是：鸭子里头，也有会自己停下来的。
story.en:
Xiaoman charged too. Among several thousand ducks, one more made no difference.

Around step one hundred and fifty his legs suddenly went heavy — not tired: as if someone had hung a millstone on each; the more he hurried, the heavier they got. Around him children sat down one after another, some panting, some crying.

At step one hundred and fifty he passed a girl with two little braids — no, it was she who passed him, charging. She didn't sit, didn't cry; charging past him, all he saw was a profile with a nose frozen red, like a radish, teeth gritted, charging up in one breath, braids flicking. That back looked a bit familiar. Xiaoman wanted a second look, but she'd already gone up; only the end of a braid flicked once in the mist, and was gone.

Step one hundred and sixty. He stopped, hands on his knees, gasping. The cliff wall was crowded with carvings — all by people who had sat down on this step. Twenty years ago his uncle had sat here the length of a stick of incense, watching others walk past him one by one.

He remembered his father's saying: chasing a deer, the more you hurry, the farther it runs. He straightened up — three steps in, three steps out; not fast, and not stopping.

With only a finger's width of incense left, he stood on the three hundredth step, legs shaking like two noodles. The old sweeper raised his eyelids and looked at him once; the look meant, roughly: even among ducks there's one that knows how to stop.
